{"content":{"id":29409,"headline":"PRISM Trial: Precision Research Integrating Symptoms and Molecular Biology in Canine Glioma","tagline":"A clinical trial to characterize the clinical disease progression in dogs with glioma","description":"

High-grade gliomas are aggressive brain tumors that are difficult to treat in dogs. While surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy may help some dogs, we still have much to learn about why some tumors respond better to treatment than others.


The purpose of this study is to better understand brain tumors in dogs by collecting information about each dog's health, MRI findings, tumor characteristics, and in some dogs, how they respond to radiation treatment. By studying many dogs with naturally occurring brain tumors, we hope to identify patterns that will help veterinarians diagnose these tumors more accurately, predict how they may behave, and develop more effective treatments in the future.


Although participation in this study may not directly benefit every dog, the information gained will help improve the care of dogs diagnosed with brain tumors and advance the development of new treatment options. Every dog that participates helps us learn more about brain tumors and brings us one step closer to improving treatment and quality of life for future dogs facing this disease.

","requirements":"

Participation in this study will last several months.

  1. An initial screening and eligibility workup, including physical and neurologic examination, blood work, and diagnostic imaging


  1. Advanced brain imaging (MRI) performed under general anesthesia


  1. Minimally invasive brain tumor biopsies performed at enrollment and after treatment


  1. Dogs that are in the palliative (no treatment) arm of the study will receive complete physical and neurological examinations, and a functional assessment every month following tumor biopsy. A brain MRI and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) collection will be performed under general anesthesia each month.


  1. Dogs that are in the radiation therapy (RT) arm of the study will receive complete physical and neurological examinations, a functional assessment, and a head CT for RT planning following the brain tumor biopsy.


  1. Overnight hospitalization following biopsy procedures


  1. Follow-up visits, including in-hospital evaluations and telemedicine check-ins


  1. Completion of owner questionnaires to monitor quality of life and treatment effects


  1. End of Study: When your family is ready to elect humane euthanasia, your dog will return to UC Davis. A brief examination will be performed prior to humane euthanasia. Following your dog’s death, a brain MRI will be performed, and they will undergo a routine necropsy. We will evaluate distribution of the drug in the brain, brain tumor, and vital organs (heart, lung, kidneys, liver). If your dog passes away or is euthanized elsewhere, the study team will arrange return to UC Davis for post-mortem evaluation.
","who_can_participate":"

Dogs may be eligible if they:

  1. Have a presumed high-grade glioma diagnosed by brain MRI
  2. Are planned to receive either palliative care or conventional fractionated radiation therapy
  3. Are otherwise healthy enough for anesthesia and repeated hospital visits
","benefits_and_risks":"

Potential Benefits:

Your dog’s participation will allow us to further understand how the molecular biology of their tumor impacts their natural lifespan and tumor growth rate, filling a critical gap in our knowledge of canine glioma biology. This important information will allow us to identify precision therapeutic approaches for glioma subtypes, provide future dog owners with a more precise prognosis, and improve the care of future dogs with glioma.


Potential Risks:

All medical procedures carry risks, including for dogs with gliomas. Your dog will undergo two (2) brain biopsies over the trial period.


General anesthesia: General anesthesia is required for brain MRI and for brain tumor biopsy, which carries inherent risk to your dog. All patients undergoing general anesthesia at the UC Davis VMC are extensively evaluated and carefully monitored during each procedure to ensure their health and safety.


Brain tumor biopsy: The biopsy procedure itself entails making a small hole in the skull and collecting 2-3 samples of tumor using a large needle. Risks associated with this procedure are low (<10% occurrence), but can include bleeding, infection, neurological decline, or even death.

If you choose to enroll your dog in this study, you will be responsible for:

  1. Covering the cost of initial diagnostic tests required to determine eligibility and any treatment your dog receives during the clinical trial period (anti-seizure medication, corticosteroids, radiation therapy)
  2. Bringing your dog to all scheduled hospital visits, treatments, imaging appointments, and follow-up evaluations
  3. Providing complete and accurate medical history and records as requested by the study team
  4. Completing quality-of-life questionnaires and participating in scheduled check-ins (including telemedicine visits)
  5. Monitoring your dog at home and promptly reporting any health changes or concerns to the study team
  6. Following all study-related instructions, including medication schedules and post-procedure care
  7. Communicating with the study team if you are unable to attend a visit or if you are considering withdrawing from the study
  8. Participation is voluntary, and you may withdraw your dog from the study at any time.
